1.open: Tell about a time someone welcomed you into their home or a group when you were new. What did they do that stuck with you?
questions: The elder writes to Gaius, "whom I love in the truth" (v. 1). What does it look like when friendship is built on something deeper than shared interests?
In verse 4 he says, "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth." Who has helped you grow in your faith, and how did they do it?

Gaius is praised as "faithful in what you are doing for the brothers," even for people who were "strangers" to him (v. 5). Why do you think welcoming strangers mattered so much for these early Christians?
Verse 8 says, "we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth." How can someone who never travels or speaks in public still share in the work of others?

Diotrephes is described as one "who loves to be first" (v. 9), and he "refuses to welcome the brothers" (v. 10). We don't know everything behind the conflict. What does the passage show about how pride can close a door?
Verse 11 says, "do not imitate what is evil, but what is good." Whose example, good or bad, has shaped how you treat other people?
Welcoming people can be tiring, awkward or costly. What honestly makes it hard for you, and what would make it a little easier?
The elder says he would rather talk "face to face" than use pen and ink (v. 14). What can a conversation in person do that a message or text cannot?
1.life: This week, welcome someone in a concrete way. Invite a newcomer to a meal, give a lift to someone who needs one, or send practical support to a missionary or traveling worker you know.
1.prayer: Thank God for the people who have opened a door for you. Ask for a humble, generous heart that notices strangers and makes room for them.
1.tip: Verse 2 is sometimes read as a promise of wealth and health for every believer. Gently point out that it is a friend's warm greeting, and keep the group focused on the chapter's main theme of hospitality. Also be fair to Diotrephes: the text gives only one side, so avoid guessing at his motives beyond what it says.
